cards.source_text: H5N1 avian influenza is spreading rapidly across southeastern Australia owing to infected wild bird species, including little penguins, magpies, crested terns and pelicans. Bird aggregations during breeding seasons will likely accelerate transmission to mammals, said Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer James Todd. In late August, H5N1 jumped to a mammal, a red fox (Vulpes vulpes), in Adelaide, South Australia. Acting chief veterinary officer Cameron Bell said that while wild foxes generally do not spread the virus directly, scavenging pests risk moving infected carcasses across habitats, according to media reports. In September, state authorities confirmed H5N1 in an Australian sea lion (Neophoca cinerea) and a common dolphin (Delphinus delphis). South Australian Environment Minister Emily Bourke said that the sea lion — a critically endangered species currently declining by 2% a year — was recovering from a shark attack when it succumbed to the virus, reports ABC Australia. Cetacean researcher Mike Bossley is concerned about how quickly a dolphin contracted the disease. In a news report, he called it both “shocking … and very worrying.” Bourke added that South Australia has recorded bird flu in another mammal species, long-nosed fur seals (Arctocephalus forsteri) and confirmed the nation’s first pelican case on the Yorke Peninsula. “The first confirmed H5N1 death recorded for [the Australian sea lion] in Australia marks a significant and worrying moment for Australian wildlife,” Bill Bateman, associate professor of behavioral ecology at Curtin University, Australia, wrote in The Conversation. He added that the evolving H5N1 strain can invade a mammal’s central nervous system, causing severe brain inflammation. The way marine mammals contract the virus is likely from birds, Bateman wrote. Sick or dead seabirds can infect coastal breeding grounds, he added, either when animals eat them or come into contact with bodily fluids or contaminated water and substrate. While there’s no “real way” to stop the spread of H5N1 now that it’s here, Bateman noted that there are ways to reduce its impact. There is a way to limit exposure, he said. “Removing carcasses safely is crucial, as it removes these viral reservoirs, and stops it getting into Australia’s many scavenging animals.” Along South Australia’s Fleurieu Peninsula, volunteers with the Victor Harbor Dolphin Watch Group are on the lookout for dolphins exhibiting abnormal swimming or neurological symptoms. cards.source_text: The caribou of Quebec are at breaking point. The province, home to 15% of Canada’s population of woodland caribou, has seen numbers crash to about half of what they were a decade ago. For years, local First Nations people, researchers and environmental groups have criticised the provincial government’s lack of action on protecting caribou, an animal considered a keystone species by Indigenous peoples. A recently announced agreement between the federal and Quebec governments has raised hopes that the province will finally be compelled to release a protection strategy. The federal government has committed C$25m (£13m) to the province for caribou over five years, with an additional C$15m for the First Nations communities on whose land the herds live. But one detail of the announcement has caused concern: the continued reliance on maternity pens. Pregnant caribou have been rounded up and enclosed in pens in the hopes that the secure environment will give them and their calves a better chance of survival. But experts say this cannot be a longterm solution. Quebec has herds throughout the province, the majority of which are woodland caribou. There are 13 woodland herds, with 6,800 to 8,900 animals in total. A caribou’s average lifespan is 10 to 15 years; females have a single calf a year, with fewer than half usually surviving their first year. The woodland herds were listed in Canada’s 2003 Species at Risk Act, but 12 of the herds are at risk of extinction in the next 20 years, says Prof Martin-Hugues St-Laurent, an animal ecologist at the University of Quebec at Rimouski. The new funding agreement focuses on only the three most critically endangered herds: in Val d’Or, Charlevoix and Gaspésie. The six remaining animals of the Val d’Or herd were placed in a protective pen in 2020, and hopes were high that the animals would breed and thrive in safety, ready for rerelease. But by summer 2026, the herd had grown by just one animal. The Charlevoix herd was penned in 2022 and numbers 48 animals; the Gaspésie herd was penned in 2023 and has 20 animals. Currently, the Val d’Or and Charlevoix herds are penned throughout the year, while it is intended that some of the Gaspésie caribou will be released every few years. cards.source_text: Major wildfires this summer in the Cairngorms, along the Suffolk coast and in the New Forest have destroyed huge swathes of important bird habitats, affecting the populations of some of our most threatened and specialised species. The first to break out, in mid-July, destroyed much of the RSPB’s Abernethy reserve, home to declining species such as black grouse and capercaillie, as well as scarce songbirds including Scottish crossbill and crested tit. Fortunately it was brought under control before it reached the village of Nethy Bridge, whose residents were briefly evacuated. In late July, there was a devastating wildfire at Dunwich Heath, on the edge of the RSPB’s showpiece Minsmere reserve in east Suffolk. Here, much of the lowland heath – one of Britain’s most globally important habitats – was totally destroyed. Three key heathland species – woodlark, Dartford warbler and nightjar – may not now return for many years. Finally, in early August, part of the New Forest – where the same three heathland species also breed – was also destroyed by a major fire. Lowland heath is especially vulnerable to wildfires as the habitat is mainly found in the warmest and driest parts of southern and eastern England. All these examples of habitat destruction and the loss of species are the consequence of the particularly hot and dry summer; itself a direct result of a rapidly heating world.

cards.source_text: One of the UK’s most precious underwater habitats – Dorset’s seagrass meadows – is recovering thanks to “eco moorings” designed to prevent the seabed being ripped up, a study has revealed. Scars caused by traditional anchors in some areas of seagrass in Studland Bay have almost entirely vanished, which is boosting the number of seahorses that thrive in the submerged meadows. The Studland Bay Marine Partnership, which includes a wide range of organisations including conservationists and boating enthusiasts, hopes the findings could help protect and restore seagrass in other busy marine environments around the UK. Seagrass meadows are considered one of the world’s most valuable ecosystems because, as well as supporting creatures such as seahorses, they store carbon and help protect coastlines from erosion. They are declining globally due to pressures including pollution, coastal development and the climate emergency. The meadows at Studland Bay are particularly at risk because the spot is so popular with leisure boaters. Research conducted by Kira Dunn, as part of her masters degree at the University of Southampton, analysed data collected since eco-moorings were installed by the partnership in 2021. In the area where 10 trial eco-moorings were installed five years ago, bare patches in the seagrass shrank by an average of 94% between 2021 and 2025. In a second study area, where traditional chain moorings remained until 2023, the scars reduced by 65%. Dunn said: “The results clearly show that seagrass is recovering in areas where physical disturbance has been removed. It’s incredibly encouraging to see how quickly this important habitat can regenerate when given the opportunity.” David Brown, the chair of the Studland Bay Marine Partnership steering group and lead ecologist for the National Trust, said: “The impact has been beyond our expectations, and thanks to robust monitoring and research, we have the science to prove how the eco-moorings benefit seagrass and all the species that rely on it.” Studland Bay was designated a marine conservation zone in 2019 and is home to one of the UK’s largest seagrass meadows, supporting numerous marine species including the protected spiny seahorse and the occasionally recorded short-snouted seahorse. Since eco-moorings were introduced volunteer divers who monitor seahorses have reported increases in numbers. cards.source_text: Researchers from India have generated reference genomes for four threatened species of Asian hornbills, reports contributor Nikhil Sreekandan for Mongabay India. The scientists from the Nature Conservation Foundation (NCF) in Mysore and the CSIR–Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB) in Hyderabad assembled high-quality genomes for threatened Asian hornbill species including the great hornbill (Buceros bicornis), rufous-necked hornbill (Aceros nipalensis), Malabar pied hornbill (Anthracoceros coronatus), and wreathed hornbill (Rhyticeros undulatus). Prior to this study, whole-genome information was available for only two of the 32 Asian hornbill species. The research team used two types of genetic sequencing to create genetic maps for each of the species; together short- and long-read DNA sequencing helped researchers minimize errors. “A genome is the complete genetic structure of an organism, [and] a reference genome is a baseline genome for a particular species,” said Pooja Pawar, corresponding author of the study and a doctoral researcher at NCF. Pawar said that genomic tools allow scientists to examine species histories across the region and over time. “I could go back in time, to when the species originated or diverged from its sister species, and not restrict [my research] to the Western Ghats or northeast India.” The team used statistical modeling to trace changes in hornbill populations over time, and discovered that climatic instability during the Pleistocene epoch (2.5 million to 11,000 years ago) reduced the effective population sizes of all four species. Among them, the widely distributed wreathed hornbill had a higher effective population size than the other three. Meghana Natesh, a conservation geneticist at WWF India who wasn’t involved in the study, said genomics also allows researchers to understand the genetic variation in populations. “Genetic variation or diversity is crucial to the adaptive potential and long-term resilience of populations,” she said. Therefore, the findings provide a foundational tool for evaluating population resilience and informing conservation management. “By comparing their genomes, we can attribute differences in their characteristics to the structural and functional variations within their genomes,” Pawar said. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 20 minute listen It is 9 am on a warm July Sunday in Cambridge, as I head towards a café in the city centre. The bells of Great St Mary’s church play the familiar melody of the Cambridge Quarters. The sound, now often associated with the chimes of Big Ben in London, was first composed here in 1793. The quarters, named for the melody at each quarter-hour, are an immediately recognisable reminder of the passage of time. Each bell produces a note: a wave with a characteristic frequency that travels through the air and reaches our ears. A hammer strikes the bell, and it oscillates, pushing air molecules back and forth. Those jostling molecules reach our ears and we hear a musical note. Then the bell settles, gives up its energy, and returns to silence. My research here at the University of Cambridge often brings me back to the ringing of a bell. I don’t study the physics of sound, but I do focus on a remarkably similar process, taking place throughout the Universe. I am interested in another object that also rings: a black hole. As I sit down with a coffee, I open my laptop to a wavy signal that gradually fades to a flat line. Two black holes have finished merging – a frenzied process of coalescence – leaving an extremely brief wiggle originating from the remnant black hole. Much like the struck bell, this leftover black hole is ringing in a process called ringdown, and it’s consistent across every merger I investigate. Ringdown allows physicists to test their theories of gravity: did Albert Einstein really have the last word? Just as an off-sounding note from a bell might indicate a design flaw, a discrepancy in the frequencies of a ringing black hole could be the first crack in our understanding of gravity. That’s the scientific rationale for studying ringdown, but what fascinates me equally is what happens next. After the black hole rings, it settles into silence. In that moment, lasting only a few milliseconds, the power and intensity of the merger are lost. From the exterior, almost all of that history suddenly becomes inaccessible, and what is left is featureless. The black hole settles into a simple, peaceful object of pure spacetime, with no trace of the violence that just happened. In some respects, the black holes forget. It seems counterintuitive that something so chaotically created can become so simple. Why do black holes seem to forget their violent histories? cards.source_text: For Abidin, a Balik elder who lives in East Kalimantan in Borneo, Indonesia, the sounds of nature aren’t merely a backdrop but a vital part of how he navigates the world. But as the rainforest around him has become more developed, the calls of creatures once heard everywhere have grown scarce. And that process is speeding up. To relieve Indonesia’s capital city of Jakarta, which is sinking due to overdevelopment and vulnerable to climate change, the government is building a new one, Nusantara, close to Abidin’s home. The noise of construction and city life is beginning to overpower the soundscape he relies on, and researchers suspect they may already be pushing wildlife away. In this short documentary, the US director Leah Varjacques traces an effort to record the sounds of the rainforest before they’re altered forever. The film follows Abidin working with a research team that includes Wendy Erb, a bioacoustic scientist from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology in New York, to collect audio from caves, treetops and everywhere in between. In doing so, they hope to create a record for posterity so that the rainforest’s soundscapes – and the culture and ancestral knowledge embedded within them – are never fully erased.

The table looked at me somewhat bemused. The local party leader leaned over to help dig me out. “They don’t have freedom,” he explained. “They don’t understand freedom.” In the two decades I spent reporting from America – 12 years as a correspondent for this paper – gun culture was one of two major issues that was difficult to translate (the other was health care). cards.source_text: “What’s in your head?” Dolores O’Riordan’s raw, plaintive refrain loops through the Cranberries’ 1994 hit Zombie. A protest song about the Troubles could, on paper, hardly seem further removed from Derek Owusu’s third novel, about a young writer recovering from a mental health crisis. But in an author’s note before The Recovery House begins, Owusu instructs the reader to listen to the song “at least two to four times before going beyond this page”. Gradually it becomes clear that the song’s central question is one Owusu’s protagonist asks in various forms throughout the novel. Can we ever fully understand what is going on in our own heads? We meet Jamal, a young novelist who has woken up in a recovery house – a residential alternative to hospital admission – after a breakdown. It transpires that he has overdosed, is an alcoholic, and has been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder. He is in a frazzled, frantic state, initially less interested in getting better than in piecing together how he got there. The house itself is hardly a sanctuary in the conventional sense: Jamal finds a single bed with protruding springs, dead cockroaches in the nightstand and restless corridors in which people in various states of distress move around one another. Jamal’s nurses watch him; he watches them back. Owusu knows the world he is writing about – he spent a summer in a recovery house himself after a mental health crisis, and there is an intimacy to the way he renders this suspended, in-between place. Writing is both Jamal’s vocation and his illness. Like Owusu, he has published two books and won an award for his first; the expectations surrounding the third have become unbearable, and he eventually remembers that it was the attempt to write it that precipitated his breakdown. He comes to the frightening realisation that “the thing that inspired me is the thing that’s trying to kill me”. Hold them too loosely and you don’t stand for anything, hold them too tightly and you become the sort of person no argument can reach. Most of us swing between the two and have no vocabulary for the ground in between. A Roman lawyer worked one out, under pressure far worse than anything we are likely to face, and it is still the best answer available. The time is early 45 BCE, the place a villa near Lucrine Lake, northwest of Naples, in southern Italy. One of the most fascinating and controversial figures in the entirety of Western history, Marcus Tullius Cicero, is finishing writing a book that will be known as the Academica, where he explains the nature of sceptical philosophy and why it is so crucial not just to the advancement of human knowledge, but to living a good life. It is a strange moment to retire into one’s villa to write. The Roman Republic, so beloved by Cicero, is about to be destroyed by aspiring autocrats: Julius Caesar, a longtime friend and now a political opponent, has declared himself dictator for life, a move that will soon lead to his assassination on the Ides of March 44 BCE. On the personal front, Cicero has recently divorced Terentia, his wife of 30 years, and a few months ago his beloved daughter Tullia died from complications following childbirth. You would think a man whose private and public worlds are collapsing so dramatically would hardly have the focus to write philosophy. Yet for Cicero such writing is a form of therapy, and the treatises he produces will influence medieval Christians, Renaissance authors, and the Founders of the American Republic. Cicero managed all this because of his adopted philosophy, ‘Academic Skepticism’, so-called because it characterised, for the period from 266 to 90 BCE, the Academy originally founded by Plato. He used to be treated as a mere populariser, a gifted Roman relaying Greek ideas he did not really own, but scholars abandoned that uncharitable verdict decades ago as it became clear that Cicero argued and decided among his sources rather than simply transcribing them. He also built a Latin philosophical vocabulary from scratch, and much of the abstract terminology of European thought descends from his coinages. In that respect, he had something in common with Vincent van Gogh, who passed most of his much shorter life in more dire circumstances. Unlike Wright, who enjoyed decades of fame at the pinnacle of the American architectural profession, van Gogh remained practically unknown until after his death. But if they’ve encountered one another in the afterlife, they’ve certainly discussed one subject above all others: their shared appreciation for Japanese woodblock prints. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured the collection of 500 such works of art that van Gogh left behind. At the end of Wright’s life in 1959, he owned about 6,000, many of which his estate had to sell to pay both Japanese art dealers and American tax collectors. We could say that Wright died as he lived, advanced age having not evidently diminished either his financial recklessness or his obsession with ukiyo‑e. The masters of that classical “art of the floating world” like Hokusai and Hiroshige were among his favorite artists of any kind. When still a teenager, Wright went to work for the architect Joseph Silsbee, who’d built a chapel for his uncle. “Silsbee’s cousin, Ernest Fenollosa, happened to be the world’s leading Western expert on Japanese art at the time,” writes Kevin Nute at The Conversation. cards.source_text: It’s an ungainly word for English speakers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gleichschaltung. Yet the concept remains central for a clear view of what happened to Germany in the 1930s. In 1933, the nation completely transformed, seemingly overnight, through “a concerted policy of ‘coordination’ (Gleichschaltung),” the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum writes. “Culture, the economy, education, and law all came under Nazi control.” Those artists and organizations that were not purged had their essential character changed to reflect an entirely different set of artistic and political values. One publication, especially, serves as an example of the Nazification of culture. The arts journal Jugend (Youth), writes Messy Nessy Chic, “had been turned largely into propaganda” between 1933 and 1940, its final year. But prior to the regime’s takeover, Jugend showcased the most avant-garde, “degenerate” artists of the era, and might have been “the ‘brainiest’ periodical of the day,” as one critic wrote in a 1904 issue of The Yale Literary Magazine. “There is no magazine published in England or in this country which is at all like it.” You can take a look yourself—browse, search, and download hundreds of scanned issues of Jugend at the University of Heidelberg’s digital archive, thousands of pages in PDF form, spanning the magazine’s forty-four-year history. You can also see images at Flickr. As in England, France, Austria, and the U.S., the Art Nouveau movement in Germany emerged from a whirlwind of post-Impressionist painting, Orientalist motifs, folk art, modernist art and advertising, book illustration, and graphic and industrial design. Appropriately, given its perch on the threshold of a new century, Art Nouveau looked both backward—to the medieval, gothic, and Romantic—and forward toward a more modernist, urbane, and urbanized sensibility. So influential was Jugend that Art Nouveau in Germany became known as Jugendstil. The Oxford Critical and Cultural History of Modernist Magazines writes, “Among Jugend’s most important qualities—indeed, an essential aspect of Art Nouveau and its German equivalent Jugendstil—was its brilliant escapism.” Founded in 1896 by writer Georg Hirth, the magazine was “from the start a venue to promote the new cultural Renaissance without recourse to the established ‘vintage’ art.” (See its very first cover right above.) cards.source_text: With the Bayeux Tapestry now on display at the British Museum, Deep Down History presents a deep dive into the embroidery’s full story: “The Bayeux Tapestry is one of the most remarkable survivals of the Middle Ages — a 70 metre embroidered account of the events leading to the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, culminating in the Battle of Hastings. This video tells the Tapestry’s story in full, using Charles Stothard’s early colour reproduction, presented here as a seamless scroll for the first time. We follow Harold Godwinson’s fateful journey from Edward the Confessor’s court to Normandy, his later seizure of the Crown, and William the Conqueror’s invasion. Beyond its political messaging, the Tapestry is also bursting with medieval history, including jokes, fascinating technical details, and a warning for those who break their promises…” Enjoy! cards.source_text: The story could scarcely be more simple: two committed patriots off to find America. The iconic, oft-referenced sequence in 1969’s psychedelic biker opera Easy Rider features the film’s twinned anti-heroes, Billy and Wyatt, tearing down a sprawling U.S. highway astride two choppers at some impossible speed, soundtracked by one of the greatest badass statements of purpose rock’n’roll ever yielded: Steppenwolf’s “Born to Be Wild.” It’s a song that perfectly bisects the dueling hippie impulses between the communitarian and utopian, and the hedonistically self-fascinated, a painful cleavage which was coming to the fore just as Easy Rider hit screens in July 1969. Can you picture it? Set against the monster rock riffs of lead guitarist Michael Monarch, singer John Kay’s edict to “take the world in a love embrace” sits nervously alongside the tune’s insinuating thirst for danger: “I like smoke and lightning/Heavy metal thunder.” This is the dichotomy that would define both the film and the soundtrack, the pastoral, pacific drop-out resistance of the Summer of Love running directly into the fraught entropy of an ersatz movement losing steam and beginning to cannibalize itself. It’s an image of such pure lawless liberation, from blue-to-red-state America, I’m not sure we’ve ever fully recovered. It’s way more “don’t tread on me” than “come on people now, smile on your brother.” In my mind—and I’ve seen the movie many, many times—I always think this is how Easy Rider starts. No score yet, be the first to add. The actual first scene in Easy Rider is intensely uneasy, a tenuous south-of-the-border drug deal that has all the hallmarks of a classic Treasure of the Sierra Madre-style misunderstanding. But no. Peter Fonda and Dennis Hopper—the film’s titular motorcycle muses—manage to fence what looks like a bumper crop of coke to a louche-looking drug connect played by Phil Spector, who sends them off with generational cash in exchange. So, the first song you hear in the movie is not Steppenwolf’s epochal nature-call, but rather their cover version of Hoyt Axton’s sad and cynical “The Pusher.” Soon enough, our heroes are unleashed, furious and stoned, on the now-decommissioned highways of 1969. But they’d never outrun the slow creeping blues of the first Steppenwolf song, even as Hopper’s Billy and Fonda’s Wyatt lit out to what was ostensibly their last deal gone down. For most of his career, that was the default Beck, the real Beck. But is that right? According to the forthcoming book The Last Temptation of Beck, he used to crash stages between sets, usually when one band was breaking down and the other was plugging in, and he’d play a few songs on acoustic guitar and harmonica for a captive audience. Some of those songs were straight-faced covers of blues standards and some were straight-faced originals, and they were generally received by a chattering crowd who were more confused than amused. It was only when Beck started rapping non sequiturs that the bystanders shut up and took notice. That was the first Beck we paid attention to, the one with the leafblower and Stormtrooper helmet, the one who announced himself on the Bong Load 7" of “Loser,” a surprise hit that caught even him off guard. The 1990s chose that Beck from several different mutations he was tinkering with at the time, and when he veered from that persona it came as a surprise. Mutations in 1998 and Sea Change in 2002 were both noteworthy for their attempts to express something personal in a more straightforward musical mode—the manchild growing up, abandoning irony and shenanigans—but those albums were just warm-ups for 2014’s Morning Phase, when Beck went full country-rock for a record that sounded like waking up after a dark night of the soul. Fans old and new embraced this new version of Beck, and none of his subsequent albums have landed with quite the same impact. Morning Phase reintroduced him as a commercially viable artist and even nabbed the Album of the Year Grammy. No score yet, be the first to add. Maybe a follow-up like Ride Lonesome was inevitable. After the more upbeat Colors in 2017 and Hyperspace in 2019, Beck once again picks up his acoustic guitar and dons his floppy folksinger hat. This version of Beck plies low-key musings about isolation and emotional alienation and arranges them in a way that balances loping country-folk with buoyant French pop (the bass is a lead instrument) and ’60s West Coast rock. Black’s second album, created with producers including Nightfeelings (Kim Petras’ Detour), Oscar Scheller (Kelela, PinkPantheress), and atlgrandma (ADÉLA, The Hellp), is full of these secret pleasure dens. It’s a giddy electro-pop concoction with frisky, hedonistic dreams, though even the most freaked-up tracks—“Exhibitionism,” “Miss Delicious,” “Waschesalon”—feel less like full-throated anthems to sexual liberation than digicam snapshots of that night you hit the sex clubs with your friends. But that’s no reason you can’t bump it in the Uber on the way to the dungeon. cards.source_text: Krallice, as a rule, do not look back. The prolific New York quartet has long been identified with the experimental black metal movement—that is, black metal carried out as a series of experiments, yielding a rich body of empirical evidence that’s been folded into their ever-evolving sound. Lev Weinstein has drummed on each of the band’s albums since 2008’s introductory Krallice, but that’s been their only true constant. Mick Barr, Colin Marston, and Nicholas McMaster have all switched instruments and traded off on vocal and songwriting duties. Dave Edwardson from Neurosis was welcomed into the fold for a few albums. Synthesizers showed up one day and, for stretches, supplanted the guitars entirely. Every step Krallice have taken has felt like a step into the unknown, until now. Scour Order, the band’s synth-free 16th full-length, returns the band to its original configuration, with Barr and Marston on guitar and McMaster on bass. It plays like Krallice’s first-ever concession to nostalgia. That isn’t a bad thing. Krallice might come off like nerdy purveyors of what was once called “thinking man’s metal,” but on their first few albums, they stacked flurries of frenetic guitar riffs and barrages of blasting drums into songs that were engaged with black metal’s original texts. Before Krallice, Barr and Marston were best known for playing in obtuse, math-y instrumental bands; they teamed up because they thought it would be fun to channel Darkthrone. As they drifted from those founding principles, the music, while always compelling, could occasionally lose some of its blood-pumping immediacy. Scour Order returns black metal to the core of Krallice. Its songs are tightly wound and doggedly riff-oriented, the sense of spaciousness on the synth-era albums all but obliterated. The compositional cleverness and destabilizing use of counterpoint that have always buoyed Krallice’s music is still evident, but it’s also clear that they’re having a blast just letting it rip. No score yet, be the first to add. That feeling arrives early and doesn’t let up. cards.source_text: Emma Ruth Rundle is discovering that there’s more to life than loneliness. Across a decade-plus of solo recordings, the Portland-based singer-songwriter has typically favored sounds of desolation and solitude. She’s treated sparse arrangements of downtuned guitars and hermetic piano chords—occasionally punctured by trudging percussion or thorny distortion—as an abandoned landscape to wander, offering meditations on trauma, death, and destruction. Her songs have often been full of the downcast thoughts you can let yourself become consumed by when you spend too long inside your own head, something that Rundle admits she’s naturally predisposed to doing. “There was a period where… I romanticized the isolated artistic hermit lifestyle a little too hard,” she said in a recent interview. “It did me more harm than good.” As Rundle worked on her new album These Killing Times, she was once again confronted with a world that disappointed her. Press materials say the record was written in early 2025 during “yet another climate disaster,” a statement that could refer to any number of cataclysmic events. But this time, when confronting the darkness, she decided she didn’t want to do it alone. Rundle worked with a hefty list of collaborators from around the world of heavy music—including avant-rock guitarist Nick Reinhart, drummer Jess Gowrie (who’s played with Chelsea Wolfe and metal band Horseneck), Baroness guitarist Gina Gleason, and her frequent collaborator Troy Zeigler, among many others. This isn’t the first time Rundle has worked with friends; she once made a memorably bleak album with the ultraprolific Louisiana metal band Thou. Still, the communitarian effort seems to have given her new energy and perspective. No score yet, be the first to add. These Killing Times cuts a particularly stark contrast to her last album, 2021’s Engine of Hell, whose stoically introspective songs bore the marks of the process that birthed them in a remote cottage in rural Wales. items.summary: From an abstract portrait of an actor who might be Natalie Portman to a groundbreaking work of autofiction, we rate the best from the coolly controversial author In Cusk’s headline-grabbing latest, a writer invents the biography of a film star who sounds very like Natalie Portman. Set in the now standard late-Cusk sans serif typeface (no frivolous flourishes!), Life of M serves up observations on fame in a light fictional coating. “To always be playing a part is to have no home.” Having made her name as a devilishly good creator of brainy social comedies, Cusk’s pivot to wintry autofiction since the Outline trilogy appears to have reached its logical conclusion in this flat, abstracted portrait of empty celebrity. The New York Times called it “rarefied, cosmopolitan, self-serious”. Sample line: “Everything I did or said in her company was false. items.summary: Gladwell’s highly readable investigation into US gun culture fails to engage with the bigger questions Once, while having a steak dinner with Republicans in a small town in Indiana, the man sitting opposite me asked: “How do you cope in London, when Muslims elected that mayor and you have all that gun control?” I’d been in enough such situations to know that there was no “winning” a conversation that starts like this and so did my best to playfully bat the question away. “Well, the Muslims didn’t elect a mayor – Londoners elected a Muslim mayor,” I said. “And we don’t talk much about gun control for the same reason we don’t talk about polar bear control: we don’t have many polar bears and we don’t have many guns.” Continue reading...

items.title: The Recovery House by Derek Owusu review – a uniquely honest view of mental health
items.summary: Writing from firsthand experience, the author offers an affecting meditation on art, mental fragility and faith “What’s in your head?” Dolores O’Riordan’s raw, plaintive refrain loops through the Cranberries’ 1994 hit Zombie. A protest song about the Troubles could, on paper, hardly seem further removed from Derek Owusu’s third novel, about a young writer recovering from a mental health crisis. But in an author’s note before The Recovery House begins, Owusu instructs the reader to listen to the song “at least two to four times before going beyond this page”. Gradually it becomes clear that the song’s central question is one Owusu’s protagonist asks in various forms throughout the novel. Can we ever fully understand what is going on in our own heads? We meet Jamal, a young novelist who has woken up in a recovery house – a residential alternative to hospital admission – after a breakdown. It transpires that he has overdosed, is an alcoholic, and has been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder. He is in a frazzled, frantic state, initially less interested in getting better than in piecing together how he got there. Continue reading...

items.title: Millions of dollars in funding but still no plan: can Quebec save its caribou from extinction?
items.summary: The Canadian government has committed C$25m to try to rescue the caribou in the province – but there is no agreement on how best to save the keystone species The caribou of Quebec are at breaking point. The province, home to 15% of Canada’s population of woodland caribou, has seen numbers crash to about half of what they were a decade ago. For years, local First Nations people, researchers and environmental groups have criticised the provincial government’s lack of action on protecting caribou, an animal considered a keystone species by Indigenous peoples. A recently announced agreement between the federal and Quebec governments has raised hopes that the province will finally be compelled to release a protection strategy. The federal government has committed C$25m (£13m) to the province for caribou over five years, with an additional C$15m for the First Nations communities on whose land the herds live. items.title: Weatherwatch: wildfires driven by global heating destroy UK bird habitats
items.summary: Hot and dry summer created conditions for fires in Scotland and England that tore through vital wildlife areas Major wildfires this summer in the Cairngorms, along the Suffolk coast and in the New Forest have destroyed huge swathes of important bird habitats, affecting the populations of some of our most threatened and specialised species. The first to break out, in mid-July, destroyed much of the RSPB ’s Abernethy reserve, home to declining species such as black grouse and capercaillie, as well as scarce songbirds including Scottish crossbill and crested tit. Fortunately it was brought under control before it reached the village of Nethy Bridge, whose residents were briefly evacuated. Continue reading...
